copy.what_it_means: One of the most persistent lawn weeds there is, spreading through chains of underground tubers that resprout even after top growth is removed. A technician evaluates the weed, turf type, season, and coverage to explain why this needs a more patient approach than an ordinary lawn weed.
copy.fact: A single tuber can produce a whole new chain of plants underground, which is why pulling the visible top growth rarely gets rid of it for good.
copy.blurb: A persistent, tuber-spreading sedge that's genuinely hard to control — often needs a different approach than an ordinary weed.

tech_notes: Underground tuber bank makes single-application control unreliable; set expectations for repeat treatment over a season or more. Per label if herbicide is used.

copy.what_it_means: A fast-growing sedge that thrives in wet or overwatered turf and spreads through underground tubers, making it more persistent than an ordinary broadleaf or grassy weed. A technician looks at the weed, irrigation and drainage, turf type, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its tubers are edible and were once cultivated as a food crop (the source of "tiger nuts"), even though in a lawn they're simply a stubborn weed.
copy.blurb: A fast-growing, tuber-spreading sedge that favors wet or overwatered turf.

tech_notes: Confirm irrigation/drainage contribution; underground tuber bank means repeat monitoring is likely needed. Per label if herbicide is used.

copy.what_it_means: A sedge that, unlike its nutsedge relatives, doesn't spread by underground tubers, which generally makes it somewhat less stubborn to manage. A technician looks at the weed, turf type, season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its seed clusters look like tiny spiky green balls, which is exactly where the name "globe sedge" comes from.
copy.blurb: A sedge with spiky, ball-like seed clusters — without the underground tubers that make nutsedge so stubborn.

tech_notes: No tuber bank, unlike Cyperus rotundus/esculentus — generally more responsive to a single well-timed approach. Per label if herbicide is used.

copy.what_it_means: A rhizome-spreading sedge that forms a dense, shiny-green mat in wet or overwatered turf, distinct from the true nutsedges since it never forms tubers. A technician looks at the weed, irrigation and drainage, turf type, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Young green kyllinga is often mistaken for one of the true nutsedges, but a dig at the base tells the story fast — kyllinga never makes tubers.
copy.blurb: A shiny, mat-forming sedge that favors wet turf — no tubers, unlike its nutsedge look-alikes.

tech_notes: Rhizome-only spread (no tuber bank) distinguishes it from Cyperus rotundus/esculentus for control planning. Per label if herbicide is used; confirm irrigation/drainage contribution.
